title: Operational shielding and postmortem playback
summary: Follow-up postmortem playback for the July 17th degraded inference incident. Reviewed root cause (prefix cache invalidation + autoscaler mispolicy), mitigation timeline, short-term shielding (rate-limits + fallback model), and longer-term reliability work (KV cache validation, autoscale hysteresis, canary rollout plan). Agreed on pilot window for resilience fixes and a benchmark run to validate latency SLOs.
topics: Root cause deep-dive: KV/prefix cache invalidation
Short-term operational shielding: rate-limits, circuit breaker, fallback models
Security/audit log requirements and compliance artifacts
Next steps and acceptance criteria for pilot
action_items: Liam Patel: produce reproducible benchmark script and runbook for KV cache invalidation test (due 2026-08-05)
Ravi Gupta: share pilot access details and schedule 2-week resilience pilot window (due 2026-08-01)
Ethan Park: provide SLO targets and traffic skeleton for benchmark (due 2026-07-31)
Caleb Brooks: confirm required audit log retention and KMS key rotation policy (due 2026-08-04)
next_steps: SE to send benchmark script and perf checklist
CSM to schedule kickoff for resilience pilot (2-week window)
Customer to sign off on acceptance criteria for canary rollouts
Redwood to share sanitized postmortem doc and links to security artifacts
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: 68 mins | Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam Patel, Ravi Gupta (Redwood) -- Sofia Morales, Ethan Park, Nina Alvarez, Caleb Brooks (BlueWard)

[00:00] Maya Chen: All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We've got about an hour, maybe a bit more, to replay the postmortem from the July 17th degradation, go over fixes, and lock down next steps. Sofia, thanks for making time.

[00:10] Sofia Morales: Yeah, thanks Maya. Appreciate you doing the playback, we wanted a crisp list of what we need to get our production SLOs back in line.

[00:24] Liam Patel: Quick intro, I'm Liam on infra at Redwood, I ran the initial repro and the perf runs. I'll go through the bench numbers and the cache behavior we saw.

[00:35] Ethan Park: just to be clear, our main concern is that latency spiked above 2s for several percentiles during peak and that our fallback path didn't activate quickly enough.

[00:48] Maya Chen: Yep that's exactly what we want to remediate. I'll start with a short timeline, then Liam will do the technical deep-dive, and then we iterate on mitigations.

[01:02] Maya Chen: Timeline — at 14:12 UTC on July 17th we saw a sustained increase in token latency. At 14:18 our autoscaler triggered additional nodes but the throughput didn't reduce as expected. At 14:34 the prefix cache hit rate dropped from 92% to sub-20% which amplified load. By 14:50 we had elevated error rates for downstream clients.

[01:30] Nina Alvarez: small note, our app-level fallback was configured but we observed a mis-typed model alias so the app didn't fall back to the cheaper L2 variant immediately, it kept routing to the primary.

[01:45] Maya Chen: Right, that aliasing thing — two parts: deployment alias mismatch and the cache invalidation window. Liam, take it.

[02:00] Liam Patel: So the repro — we instrumented a traffic replay using customer-provided traces and a synthetic traffic generator. The primary failure mode was that under high churn (many short-lived chat sessions) the KV cache eviction logic on the serving nodes dropped prefix keys prematurely. We saw rapid cache churn when session churn exceeded our assumptions. That led to many cold KV cache misses which pushed the runtime into synchronous fetches and bigger latencies.

[02:35] Ethan Park: when you say KV cache did you mean the prefix store? I think logs had "K-V cash" in them, which made us laugh but also made parsing harder.

[02:44] Liam Patel: Yeah, logs are messy, sometimes it prints "K V cash" — transcription stuff. But it's the prefix/kv store. Two issues: the eviction policy was a simple LRU and it's not eviction-aware of pinned keys used by long-running sessions, and second the autoscaler reacts quickly but without hysteresis so new nodes spin up and then immediately scale down, thrashing cache warming.

[03:12] Maya Chen: So root cause summary: cache invalidation + autoscale hysteresis gap + model alias misrouting (app side). That combined to remove the cheap prefix hits and increase token cost and latency.

[03:35] Ravi Gupta: Also, a small note from ops: our telemetry didn't flag the cache miss spike early enough because of sampling and because the per-token telemetry was aggregated at 60s buckets. We missed the early signal.

[03:56] Sofia Morales: OK, curious on mitigations — what did you do live and what should we do short-term?

[04:05] Maya Chen: In-prod mitigations deployed July 17th: 1) throttled ingestion at the edge for noisy endpoints, 2) drove a manual alias rollback to the L2 model for high-latency routes, and 3) adjusted the autoscale policy to hold for 3 minutes before downscaling. Those got us back to stable by ~16:10.

[04:34] Ethan Park: The manual alias rollback was, uh, tense — we want automated fallback in future.

[04:41] Maya Chen: Understood. Proposed short-term shielding: automated fallback policy with explicit alias priority, a circuit-breaker that trips to L2 after p95 > 1.2s for 2 mins, and a temporary prefix-key pinning for hot sessions (server-side TTL bump).

[05:05] Nina Alvarez: For circuit-breaker thresholds we'll need to align on customer SLOs — our SLO is p95 <= 800ms, p99 <= 1.5s.

[05:18] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll use those numbers as acceptance criteria for pilot.

[05:27] Liam Patel: Long-term fixes we recommend: 1) make the eviction policy workload-aware (segmented LRU with pinned key buckets), 2) autoscaler hysteresis improvement (hold and sample cache warmth before scale-down), 3) add bloom-filter style warm-check to reduce cold k/v fetches, 4) improved telemetry with sub-10s window and anomaly alerts.

[05:54] Caleb Brooks: On security/compliance: we need the sanitized audit logs for the pilot, and we need assurances about encryption at rest for any persisted cache shards. Also rotation window for KMS keys.

[06:10] Liam Patel: All cache shards are encrypted with AES-256 and KMS-managed keys. We'll share a short security artifact pack. For the audit logs we can provide redacted timeline logs and retention policy (we recommended 90 days).

[06:25] Maya Chen: We'll link the security doc — link: https://redwood.example.com/security/blueward-auditpack (sanitized) — we'll send after the call.

[06:35] Sofia Morales: Good. Walk me through the benchmark plan. I want to be absolutely sure the fix prevents recurrence.

[06:42] Liam Patel: Benchmark plan: 1) replay live traces at 1.2x peak for 30 minutes, 2) introduce session churn bursts (short sessions 3-10 tokens), 3) measure p50/p95/p99 and cache hit rate every 10s, 4) run with proposed eviction policy and with current to compare. We'll include a script and runbook.

[07:05] Ethan Park: Can you also run it with a simulated network hiccup (5% packet loss) to see how the autoscaler reacts? That was a factor in our edge region last month.

[07:16] Liam Patel: Yep we can simulate packet loss and increased RT. We'll add it to the matrix.

[07:25] Maya Chen: Let's talk about ownership and timelines. We propose a 2-week pilot: week 1 run benchmarks and deploy autoscale hysteresis + circuit breaker in staging; week 2 run canary on 10% traffic and observe SLOs; if green, expand. Ravi, you'll coordinate.

[07:44] Ravi Gupta: Yep I'll set up the pilot schedule. Proposed dates: August 3rd - August 16th. Does that align with BlueWard?

[07:53] Sofia Morales: That works for us, subject to internal sign-off. We may need a security review with Caleb before starting.

[08:02] Caleb Brooks: I'll do a quick review. For the audit artifact I need the retention and redaction approach spelled out. Also want a promise of no user PII in logs.

[08:15] Maya Chen: Confirmed — we'll sanitize and exclude PII, and we'll provide a redaction checklist.

[08:24] Nina Alvarez: Quick question on cost: switching to L2 model reduces token cost by ~40% but might change quality for some routes. How do we ensure quality guardrails?

[08:36] Liam Patel: We recommend a hybrid approach: for high-confidence deterministic routes we can use L2; for sensitive generative flows, keep L1 but enforce soft-thresholds. We'll also produce a small evaluation set to ensure quality delta is acceptable.

[08:56] Ethan Park: Who signs off on the quality evaluation? Product or engineering?

[09:02] Nina Alvarez: Product owns quality gating, engineering owns SLOs. We'll sign off together.

[09:10] Maya Chen: Great. Now I'm going to read through the postmortem doc live — I'll paraphrase and then we can annotate. Link to postmortem: https://drive.example.com/blueward-postmortem-july17 (redacted).

[09:24] Maya Chen: (reading) Sequence: high session churn -> cache eviction -> cold KV misses -> autoscaler thrash -> elevated latency -> fallback misrouting -> client errors. Notes: sampling buckets hid initial spike.

[09:45] Ethan Park: That sampling bit — can we get higher resolution metrics pushed to us, even if it's sample-sparse? The 60s aggregation was too coarse.

[09:56] Ravi Gupta: We'll enable 10s buckets for the pilot and expose them to your SRE team via prometheus endpoint.

[10:04] Sofia Morales: Cool. A few clarifying Qs: 1) How long does prefix key pinning hold? 2) What's the rollback plan if the canary fails?

[10:12] Liam Patel: Pinning TTL proposed is 5 minutes for hot sessions; it can be tuned. Rollback plan: immediate routing to previous autoscale policy and model alias; also scaling down canary traffic to 0% and reverting any config flags. We'll have a runbook with play steps.

[10:32] Maya Chen: Now the SE bench numbers — Liam?

[10:35] Liam Patel: Baseline (pre-incident) p95 = 620ms, p99 = 990ms, cache hit ~92%. Incident run p95 = 1.3s, p99 = 2.6s, cache hit ~18%. With pinned TTL and hysteresis we get p95 ~680ms, p99 ~1.1s and cache hit ~85% in our synthetic runs. Those are preliminary but promising.

[11:01] Ethan Park: The p99 at 1.1s is slightly above our p99 target but acceptable if p95 is within goal. Need to watch p99.

[11:10] Maya Chen: For acceptance criteria of pilot let's set: p95 <= 800ms and p99 <= 1.4s under 1.2x peak replay. If those are met, expand.

[11:22] Sofia Morales: Agreed. Now security specifics — Caleb?

[11:26] Caleb Brooks: We need SOC2 type references, KMS rotation frequency, and confirmation that any temporary logs for debugging are ephemeral and will be deleted after 30 days. Also want to see RBAC for console access.

[11:39] Maya Chen: We'll share SOC2 summary (link), KMS rotation schedule, and RBAC audit. We'll redact PII.

[11:48] Caleb Brooks: Also can we restrict debug-level logs to the pilot window only and have an expiration?

[11:54] Ravi Gupta: Yes, debug logs will be enabled for the pilot and automatically pruned after 30 days. We'll document the process.

[12:02] Nina Alvarez: Thinking about the canary expansion — what traffic steering approach do you use? Weighted proxy or per-route?

[12:10] Liam Patel: We use per-route weighted steering via our gateway. We can target only the problem routes for canary, or roll up by percentage. Per-route gives safer rollback granularity.

[12:24] Maya Chen: Any blockers from BlueWard on the plan? Sofia?

[12:29] Sofia Morales: Main blocker is internal security sign-off. Otherwise we have alignment. We also need a customer-facing incident summary for executives. Can you provide a one-page exec summary?

[12:41] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll produce an executive summary and a timeline artifact.

[12:47] Ethan Park: One more operational ask — can we have an SLA credit proposal if the pilot misses SLOs due to platform regressions? We want clarity on remediation.

[12:55] Maya Chen: I'll loop in account team after the call; we can draft a temporary SLA credit proposal for the pilot window. Not a full legal commitment, but a path to credits if platform issues cause missed SLOs.

[13:10] Sofia Morales: Sounds fair. OK, let's capture explicit next steps.

[13:16] Maya Chen: I'll read action items aloud: 1) Liam to share benchmark script & runbook (due Aug 5). 2) Ravi to schedule pilot (Aug 3-16). 3) Caleb to confirm audit requirements (Aug 4). 4) Ethan to share SLO skeleton and traffic traces (Jul 31). 5) Redwood to provide exec summary and sanitized postmortem link (by Aug 2). Any corrections?

[13:45] Sofia Morales: Add that we want test matrix to include packet loss sim.

[13:50] Liam Patel: noted, will include packet loss and churn bursts.

[13:56] Maya Chen: Great. Final Qs?

[14:02] Nina Alvarez: Will Redwood run the canary or do we expect BlueWard to drive it?

[14:08] Ravi Gupta: Redwood will run the canary in coordination with BlueWard — we'll need an ops contact to approve roll/unroll, likely Ethan.

[14:16] Ethan Park: Yeah I'll be the approver.

[14:20] Maya Chen: OK. Closing recap: pilot dates Aug 3-16; acceptance p95 <=800ms p99 <=1.4s at 1.2x peak; audit artifacts and exec summary to be delivered; benchmark script and runbook by Aug 5.

[14:40] Sofia Morales: Thanks, that's all from me. Appreciate the thoroughness.

[14:46] Caleb Brooks: Thanks everyone.

[14:49] Maya Chen: We'll follow up in email with links and calendar invites. Meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcription: multiple places showed garbled tokens ("K-V cash"), occasional speaker mis-attribution in auto-transcript, and some timestamps approximated. The team flagged that the postmortem doc will be the canonical source of truth.

Shared artifacts: https://drive.example.com/blueward-postmortem-july17 (postmortem), https://redwood.example.com/security/blueward-auditpack (security artifacts), https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/blueward-kv-repro (benchmark scripts, pending upload).

End of transcript.

Can Redwood simulate packet loss during benchmarks? (Answer: yes)
Who will approve canary rollouts? (Answer: Ethan Park)
